title: The collar
hook: a man rages against his vocation until he hears "Child!" and answers "My Lord" (The Collar)
tomorrow: can sweeping a floor be a prayer? Herbert has a line for that.

segments.voice: The camp's last week, in lines: light on the moss; the southern mountain; cold mountain; so I did sit and eat; restlessness. And yesterday's: something understood.

Some days end with a message typed and deleted: I quit. George Herbert wrote a poem that starts right there. "I struck the board, and cried, No more. I will abroad." He wants out. His life feels like a cage, his harvest only thorns. And the lines run ragged and loud, one complaint tumbling over the next.

segments.voice: Herbert had hoped for a life at court, Walton tells, before he became a country priest, and some readers hear that in The Collar. Even the title has more than one sound: a priest's collar, a collar that holds you back, and some readers hear choler, an old word for anger. The poem lets the anger run, uneven and wild. Then: "But as I rav'd and grew more fierce and wild At every word, Methought I heard one calling, Child! And I replied, My Lord." One word, and the rage is answered, not argued with. That's the Christian teaching of adoption: God calls people children, not just servants. Paul writes in Romans: "ye have received the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father." Herbert's rage isn't punished. It's met with a name. And that closes this camp of poets, from Tagore's butterfly and Basho's road to Issa's dew, Li Bai's moon and Herbert's table.
screen: `A COLLAR, OR CHOLER.` · `THE RAGE RUNS.` · `ONE CALLING: CHILD!` · `THE SPIRIT OF ADOPTION.` · then, large: `CHILD.`

segments.voice: Make two fists, and feel what's tight in you today: a grievance, a no more. Hold it for one breath. Then open your hands, palms up, and leave them resting open while you sit. Nothing to fix; let one rage settle.
The collar: Herbert's poem of a man raging against his calling, until one word calls him back.
Your line: child. The rage runs, and a name answers it. Twenty-one of twenty-one, camp done.

howItsDone: Christians call God Father and speak of being adopted as God's children (Romans 8:15). Herbert's The Collar is read as a prayer that lets anger be said before it is answered.
